So basically, they're emulating the entire Xbox 360 console with a virtual machine running on top of the Xbone software.

Neat-o. Slim chance of that happening with PS4. I imagine trying to emulate a cell architecture would be miles harder than emulating PPC, which was a feat in itself.
the xbone is built around a virual machine and is running 3 os's already, it'd be interesting to see how this new addition effect the already weak performance.
Huh? It loads the 360 VM when you launch a 360 game. It's not consuming any resources at any other time.

The primary OS, the hypervisor, the first thing that boots, doesn't use hardly any resources, as it's just there to maintain the other VMs. The other two VMs are the Apps portion, and the Games portion, and it sounds like the 360 emulator might be its own VM as well. Keep in mind that the hypervisor can adjust resource usage at any given time, the 360 VM will take the place of the Games VM when you're using the 360, and vice-versa. It shouldn't affect performance for apps and games at all, as it'll sit dormant when it's not being used. Apps that run simultaneously to the 360 game may be affected somewhat, if the 360 emulator uses more resources than a One game, but with app switching, the system can pause the game in the 360 VM and ramp down its resources accordingly. While I'm a PS4 fan, as a systems administrator, the VM-based architecture of the One is pretty nifty.

It's even a little more simple than that. The 360 VM is treated as an X1 game. So you can have the 360 VM running alongside apps, but as soon as you launch any other game, the 360 VM resources are dumped. It's the same as if you're playing Sunset Overdrive then switch to Garden Warfare. SO isn't keeping any resources, they're all freed up for GW. Down in the weeds it's certainly more complicated, but you can see this happening when you launch a 360 game. You get the full 360 boot sequence, startup animation/sounds and all, but it goes immediately into the game rather than the 360 dash.

The only point of me adding this is really to note that the 360 BC isn't consuming any resources when you aren't playing a 360 game. It's just another application sitting on disk.

And I'm with you on digging the architecture of the X1. I waffle between thinking it's overkill and thinking it's got potential for providing some real flexibility in the future. Regardless, it's cool.

This is actually what the Wii U does already. It has a Wii emulator built in which allows it to run Wii disks and digital downloads. Considering how much less powerful the Wii U is compared to the Xbone, I suspect it should work very well. I am a little disappointed that Microsoft isn't going to take advantage of using an emulator to also grant visual and performance improvements to the last-gen titles, but I guess stability should be the highest priority.

The Wii U is based on similar architecture to the Wii though, just as the Wii was built on the GameCube, the Wii software can run almost natively on the Wii U hardware, given a hypervisor. This 360-to-One transition is straight up insane from an architectural standpoint, they're completely different.
That's interesting, I didn't think there would be a big difference since they are both basically Windows OS systems. Do you know specifically what is different about the architecture?

It has to do with the layer of emulation that MS is going for. With the 360, they were emulating an x86 on a PPC, which is really hard to do with gaming-level performance, but they got around it by essentially making a minimal version of the original Xbox OS for PPC, translating API calls at that layer. They're emulating the 360 in a completely different manner, if this information is correct, in that they're creating software that runs the 360 OS in its original form, emulating lower-level hardware calls as well as the higher-level API calls. This provides more compatibility than the "shim" method used in the 360 for the original Xbox, as many games access the hardware at a lower level, but at the cost of performance, usually.

Interesting that they're going OS level with this. I assumed that, given Microsoft's proficiency for APIs, they'd be doing a shim again, emulating a tri-core PPC and an 11 year old ATI graphics card with low-level calls (assuming that it's not all abstracted through directx, it might be) on an x86-based architecture with a modern ATI card seems kind of insane, frankly.
